title: Prunes: fiber, sugar and nutritional value

seo.title: Prunes: fiber, sugar, calories and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Prunes provide about 7.1 g of fiber and 38 g of sugars per 100 g. See a 30-g serving and why prunes are associated with bowel regularity.
seo.search_intent: Learn the fiber, sugar, calorie and nutrient content of prunes and understand why they are associated with bowel regularity.

excerpt: Prunes concentrate nutrients and sugars as fresh plums lose water. Per 100 g they provide about 240 calories, 38 g of sugars and 7.1 g of fiber. A 30-g serving—roughly four to five prunes depending on size—has about 72 calories, 11 g of sugars and 2.1 g of fiber. Their effect on bowel function is not just about fiber; prunes also contain sorbitol and other fruit compounds.
content_html:
Prunes have an unusually specific reputation: people buy them as much for “regularity” as for flavor. That reputation has a nutritional basis, but it helps to start with what is actually in a serving. Prunes are dried fruit, so fiber and sugars arrive together in concentrated form.

What 100 grams of prunes contains

USDA reference values put 100 g of prunes at about 240 calories, 64 g of carbohydrate, 38 g of sugars, and 7.1 g of fiber. They also provide potassium, vitamin K, and a variety of phenolic compounds.

PrunesPer 100 gPer 30 g
Energy≈240 kcal≈72 kcal
Sugars≈38 g≈11.4 g
Fiber≈7.1 g≈2.1 g

The 30-g column is more useful for a snack. Depending on size, that is roughly four or five prunes: enough to provide a little over 2 g of fiber without approaching the 240 calories in a 100-g portion.

Prunes are lower in sugar than some dried fruits

Prunes contain about 38 g of sugars per 100 g, compared with roughly 59 g/100 g in raisins and 66–67 g/100 g in Medjool dates. That does not make prunes low-sugar; they are still a concentrated carbohydrate food.

Part of the difference comes from their carbohydrate profile. Prunes naturally contain sorbitol, a sugar alcohol that contributes sweetness and behaves differently in the digestive tract from glucose or sucrose.

Fiber is not working alone

The 7.1 g of fiber per 100 g can add bulk and change stool consistency. Sorbitol is incompletely absorbed and can draw water into the intestine. Phenolic compounds and the fruit matrix may contribute as well.

Clinical research on prunes has found improvements in stool frequency and consistency in some groups. That does not turn prunes into a universal dose-dependent remedy; bowel habits also depend on total diet, fluids, activity, medications, and health conditions.

More is not always more comfortable

Someone who jumps from no prunes to a large portion may notice gas, bloating, or loose stools because both fiber and sorbitol increase at once. Starting with about 20–30 g makes it easier to judge individual tolerance.

Adequate fluids and fiber from a range of foods are generally more practical than relying on one dried fruit to carry the entire job.

How prunes fit into an everyday diet

Four or five prunes can be paired with yogurt, oatmeal, nuts, or savory dishes. Their sweetness can also reduce the need for some added sugar in recipes, although the fruit still contributes its own naturally occurring sugars.

The balanced read is that prunes provide a useful amount of fiber for a small food and have a carbohydrate profile relevant to bowel regularity, while remaining energy-dense dried fruit. A visible 30-g serving is easier to interpret than eating from the bag.

faq.question: How much fiber is in prunes?
faq.answer: About 7.1 g per 100 g. A 30-g serving provides roughly 2.1 g of fiber.

faq.question: How much sugar is in prunes?
faq.answer: They contain about 38 g of sugars per 100 g, or roughly 11 g in a 30-g serving.

faq.question: Why can prunes help with regularity?
faq.answer: They combine fiber with naturally occurring sorbitol and other fruit compounds. The effect and tolerance vary by portion and individual.
